items.title: Republicans put Trump centre stage in US midterms gamble
items.description: US Republicans open an extraordinary midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday, betting that putting Donald Trump at the centre of their campaign can rescue a party facing grim election forecasts — despite the president’s deeply negative approval ratings. The two-day gathering, dubbed “Trumpapalooza,” is designed to persuade the Republican leader’s supporters that he is effectively on the ballot on November 3, when Republicans risk losing the House of Representatives and face a fierce fight to retain the Senate. “So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” Trump said recently at a rally in South Carolina. “Just come and vote. It’s so important.” Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats to win the House 230-205 and the Senate to finish 51-49 in their favour — revising its 50-50 prediction as the outlook continues to worsen for Republicans. Trump, whose approval rating stood at just 33 per cent in recent polling , will speak on both convention nights at the American Airlines Centre. U.S. President Donald Trump walks to board Marine One, en route to Dallas, Texas, at the Ellipse near the White House in Washington, DC, the US on September 9, 2026. — Reuters His challenge is to mobilise voters personally loyal to him without further alienating independents already souring on his presidency amid inflation woes, gasoline prices topping $4 a gallon and the continuing war on Iran . “Many Trump supporters only vote when he’s on the ballot,” Matthew Green, a politics professor at the Catholic University of America, told AFP . “They’re not diehard Republican voters; they’re diehard Trump voters. So, in that respect, it makes some sense to feature Trump in the hopes of getting those folks to turn out in November.” But Green was sceptical that asking those supporters to imagine Trump on their ballots could overcome his broader weakness. “When you’re in the low- to mid-30s, that’s traditionally associated with a very bad midterm for your party,” he said of the 80-year-old’s approval ratings. Trump show The gathering is the first Republican national convention held specifically for a midterm election, although no candidates will be nominated and no formal party business is planned. Instead, organisers have constructed what amounts to a two-night television rally touting Trump’s record and Republican candidates. More than 100 House members and candidates are expected, with over 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night. Rubber ducks shaped as US President Donald Trump are seen at a store outside of the American Airlines Centre ahead of the 2026 Republican National Committee (RNC) Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas on September 08, 2026. — AFP Trump delivers Wednesday’s keynote and returns for Thursday’s finale after Vice President JD Vance speaks. Cabinet members, congressional leaders and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the program. Republicans plan to highlight tax cuts, immigration enforcement, manufacturing and prescription drug prices, while depicting Democrats as dangerously far to the left. Some Republicans, however, are privately hoping Trump sticks to that script rather than the personal grievances and off-message subjects that regularly dominate his appearances. Staying home Not everyone is coming. Numerous lawmakers in competitive races have decided that, less than two months from Election Day, their time is better spent campaigning at home. House Speaker Mike Johnson has acknowledged the dilemma, saying some members need to remain home because it is a “critical time” immediately before early voting accelerates nationwide. And even Trump’s promised national television showcase faces an unusually formidable rival. Both convention nights coincide with the opening games of the NFL season. “Spending three or four days away from your district to go to a convention is not a good way to spend your time if you’re facing a tight re-election,” Green added. Democrats were also making their presence felt in Dallas, with the party sending out some of its most high-profile speakers for public events. “Americans are being crushed by rising costs,” Colorado Congressman Jason Crow posted on X. “Republicans don’t care — they’re in Dallas, celebrating an out-of-touch President whose tariffs and wars are making things worse. We’re going to hold them accountable.”

items.title: SDP ratifies convention committee, targets 2027 victory
items.description: … Party says it will unite Nigeria, defeat poverty through grassroots mobilisation By Henry Umoru ABUJA — The Social Democratic Party, SDP, has held its National Convention in Abuja, ratifying the election of Professor Sadiq Gombe as Chairman of the Convention Committee, Dr Olu Agunloye as Secretary and Hon. Mulikat Adeola-Akande as Deputy Chairman, among other members. The convention, held on Wednesday at Newton Park Hotel, Abuja, also ratified decisions of the party’s National Working Committee, NWC, and National Executive Committee, NEC, directing relevant organs to take disciplinary action against members allegedly involved in unauthorised membership registers, meetings and nominations. The convention was held under the theme, “Consolidating the Blueprint for a New Nigeria to Secure Homeland and Defeat Poverty.” Speaking at the event, SDP National Chairman, Prof. Sadiq Gombe, declared that the party remained “strong, organised and united”, with structures from the national to the ward level intact and ready for the 2027 presidential and general elections. Gombe urged members to put internal distractions behind them and focus on strengthening the party ahead of the presidential, National Assembly, governorship and State House of Assembly elections. He also called on members to move from consultation to mobilisation by strengthening the party’s structures from the polling units upward, with greater emphasis on youths and women. “The time has come to move from consultation to mobilisation. Every member must return to the grassroots and strengthen our structures from the polling unit upward,” he said. Gombe said that despite the challenges confronting the party, the SDP remained committed to due process, its constitution, the Electoral Act and the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. “The SDP was founded on social justice, equity, fairness, inclusion and equal opportunities. Political power must be used to transform society, uplift the people and restore hope to Nigerians,” he said. Adebayo: SDP will unite Nigeria, defeat poverty The SDP presidential candidate, Prince Adewole Adebayo, said the party would unite Nigerians, tackle poverty and insecurity and build a country that citizens could be proud of if elected in 2027. Adebayo said the SDP was founded to serve the people rather than individuals, adding that leadership should be measured by the ability to solve the problems confronting citizens. “Leadership is not about occupying public office. Leadership is about accepting the responsibility of solving the problems of the people,” he said. He maintained that Nigeria had sufficient natural resources to prosper and urged voters to support leaders with the capacity and commitment to transform the country. Recalling the history of the SDP, Adebayo said the party produced the late Chief Moshood Abiola as its presidential candidate in the 1993 election, but the election was annulled and the party subsequently banned. “Today we are back to complete what we started: to end poverty and insecurity,” he said. According to him, the SDP was different from other political parties. “The only thing we share with them is INEC. This party is not for self-glorification. We are here to fix the country,” he said. Adebayo attributed many of Nigeria’s challenges to poor leadership rather than a lack of natural resources. “We have oil, gas and minerals that no civilisation in history has had. God did not create Nigeria to be poor,” he said. He also called for the election of a National Assembly that would reflect Nigeria’s diversity and remain connected to constituents. “We need representatives who go to Abuja to listen to their brothers and solve problems, not to take,” he said. The presidential candidate urged party members to commence sustained door-to-door mobilisation across their communities, stressing that winning the 2027 elections would require first winning the confidence of Nigerians. “Nigerians are tired of excuses. They want change. They want to live without fear of insecurity,” he said. “Our mission is simple: farewell to poverty and insecurity. Let us stamp our generation’s name in history.” Bugaje urges members to preserve SDP identity The SDP vice-presidential candidate, Dr Usman Bugaje, urged members to preserve the identity of the party, saying its strength should be measured by its ideas, integrity and ability to provide solutions to Nigeria’s challenges. “The strength of the SDP is not in big men. It is in our ideas, our integrity, our honesty and our capacity to provide solutions to the problems confronting Nigerians,” Bugaje said. He warned that Nigeria could not afford further political failure, stressing the need for innovative ideas, sacrifice and responsible leadership to address the country’s challenges. Also speaking, Chairman of the Forum of SDP State Chairmen, Femi Olaniyi, urged members to strengthen party structures in their respective states rather than depend on the national secretariat in Abuja. “The strength of this party must come from the states and the grassroots. We cannot build the SDP by depending on Abuja,” he said. Olaniyi also commended Adebayo for his financial and moral support for the party. Speaking on behalf of the governorship candidates, former Inspector-General of Police and SDP governorship candidate in Nasarawa State, Mohammed Adamu, urged supporters and state chairmen to return to their communities, mobilise voters and support the party’s candidates. Representing SDP candidates for the National Assembly and State Houses of Assembly, Solomon Akwashiki called for aggressive grassroots mobilisation to enable the party secure a strong presence in the legislatures. “We must take the SDP to every community, every ward and every polling unit if we are serious about winning in 2027,” he said. Also speaking, Prophet Isa El-Buba urged SDP leaders and members to remain committed to the party’s ideals, saying no amount of money was worth compromising their conscience. “No amount of money is worth selling your conscience. We must remain committed to the struggle to end poverty and insecurity in Nigeria,” he said. He called for sacrifice and commitment, particularly in addressing poverty and insecurity in Northern Nigeria, while urging the party leadership to remain disciplined, focused and non-sentimental. items.description: Court remands suspect in correctional facility By Kingsley Omonobi ABUJA — Operatives of the FCT Police Command have arrested a woman, Mrs Beauty Monday, for allegedly pouring boiling water on her neighbour during an argument in the Lugbe area of Abuja. The command’s spokesperson, SP Josephine Adeh, disclosed this in a statement on Wednesday. Adeh said the command received a report at the Lugbe Police Division on September 6 from the victim, identified as Gift Amos, alleging that Monday poured a pot of boiling water on her back during an argument on September 4. “The FCT Police Command, on the 6th of September 2026, at about 3:30pm, received a report at Lugbe Police Division from one Gift Amos of Lugbe, FCT, alleging that on the 4th of September 2026, she had an argument with her neighbour, one Mrs Beauty Monday, during which the suspect poured a pot of boiling water on her back, causing serious burns and grievous hurt,” she said. According to the police, preliminary investigation showed that the incident followed an argument over the use of a shared compound space. Adeh said the victim had moved the suspect’s pot of boiling water from the stove to the portion of the compound allocated to her, an action which allegedly angered the suspect. “The action angered the suspect, who subsequently removed the pot from the stove and poured the boiling water on the victim’s back,” she said. The victim is currently receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained in the incident, the police said. Adeh added that the suspect had been arraigned before a court and remanded at the Suleja Correctional Centre pending further proceedings. She said the matter had been adjourned until September 16, 2026. The Commissioner of Police, FCT Command, CP Ahmed Muhammed Sanusi, urged residents to embrace peaceful coexistence and exercise restraint in resolving disagreements. Sanusi also cautioned residents against resorting to violence or self-help when faced with disputes, urging them to use lawful and peaceful means of resolving conflicts. The command further advised residents to remain vigilant and promptly report suspicious persons or activities to the nearest police station or through its emergency lines. The post FCT Police arrest woman over boiling water attack appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Tongue routs Pakistan as England dominate in third Test
items.description: England are on course to complete a series whitewash after Pakistan’s brittle batting collapsed again on the opening day of the third Test at Edgbaston on Wednesday. The tourists, who have failed to reach 200 in the series, were dismantled once more by England’s four-man pace attack and were shot out for 133 in just 33.5 overs. Josh Tongue led the way with 4-42 with Ollie Robinson taking 3-15 and Jofra Archer 3-25. Debutant Razaullah enjoyed a dream start to his Pakistan test career, taking the prize wicket of Joe Root with his fourth ball, but a century stand from Emilio Gay and Harry Brook put England in command. They closed with a lead of 23 on 156-4. Razaullah, 21, was one of three new caps, along with wicketkeeper Ghazi Ghori and Mohammad Imran, in a Pakistan side thrown into chaos when seven players were sent home after the second test loss at Lords. Coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and his assistant Umar Gul were also sacked in the aftermath. The pattern of the series was maintained with Pakistan getting away to another awful start after being put in to bat, slumping to 26-4 inside the opening hour. Saim Ayub, recalled after a 21-month absence, was trapped lbw by Robinson, giving the Sussex captain his 100th Test wicket in his 24th test, and opening partner Azan Awais was caught by a diving Tongue at wide mid-on off Archer for nine. Abdullah Shafique followed, caught well low down to his left at gully by Dan Lawrence off Robinson for three. When Shan Masood miscued a pull to mid-on off Archer, the tourists were reeling. Pakistan’s problems mounted when Tongue was introduced. He bowled Pakistan captain Babar Azam in his first over for seven, trapped Ghazi for four before yorking Imran for five. At lunch Pakistan were in disarray at 100-7. Razaullah lasted just three balls after the resumption, edging Robinson to Ben Duckett who made amends for two earlier spills with the catch. Saud Shakeel, who hit 97 at Lords, top-scored again with 43 from 47 balls before becoming Tongue’s fourth victim. It said much about Pakistan’s limp effort that the highest partnership of the innings was the last-wicket stand of 26 between Mohammad Abbas, who made 21, and Mohammad Ali. England did not have it all their own way when their turn came on a surface offering some help to the bowlers with Ali and Abbas nipping out Duckett and Jordan Cox respectively early on. When Root fell lbw for the ninth time in his last 12 test innings, England were 39-3 but Brook and Gay restored order. For Gay, still establishing himself in the England side, his highest Test score of 60 from 114 balls was an important contribution. He exited late on, dragging on a ball from the impressive Razaullah, who touched 90mph, but Brook will be at the crease on 52 tomorrow morning alongside Lawrence.

items.title: 2027: Kalu mobilises diaspora support for Tinubu, Hamzat
items.description: Senator faults calls for return of fuel subsidy, urges focus on security, economic growth By Kenneth Udeh, Abuja ABUJA — Senator representing Abia North, Orji Uzor Kalu, has urged Nigerians in the Diaspora to support President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration and the All Progressives Congress, APC, ahead of the 2027 elections, while opposing calls for the return of petroleum subsidy. Kalu also canvassed support for the Deputy Governor of Lagos State, Dr Obafemi Hamzat, as the state’s next governor. The former Abia State governor spoke on Wednesday in Maryland, United States, where he was hosted by a cross-section of Nigerians and Lagos indigenes in the Diaspora. He fielded questions on the state of the Nigerian economy, the Tinubu administration’s reforms and the country’s political direction. Kalu, who chairs the Senate Committee on the South East Development Commission, SEDC, and is seeking re-election on the APC platform, described Hamzat as a competent choice to lead Lagos. According to him, Hamzat’s long experience in the Lagos State Government had given him a strong understanding of governance and Nigeria’s diverse population. “Governor, the Deputy Governor of Lagos State, Dr Obafemi Hamzat, is a good choice. Yes, in kind, in person, in mind, and in everything. “He has been in the government of Lagos State from 2006 till today. He understands government, he understands our people, he understands Nigeria, he understands the Yorubas, he understands the Hausas and the Igbos,” Kalu said. He expressed confidence that Hamzat would contribute to building what he described as a “new Lagos” and “new Nigeria”, where citizens would have a greater sense of belonging. Kalu defends Tinubu’s reforms On the Federal Government’s economic policies, Kalu said Nigerians needed to understand that fundamental economic reforms could not produce their full benefits overnight. He said Tinubu had taken difficult decisions aimed at stabilising the economy, comparing the process with reforms undertaken in countries such as Singapore. “I will deviate a little bit to speak and talk about our President. It’s very difficult to do reforms. Today, you see people celebrating today that he did a reform that is one of the best in Singapore. Yes, it’s true. But it took years!” he said. Kalu, who disclosed that he contested the presidency in 2007 before stepping down, said his political experience had given him an understanding of the challenges involved in governing Nigeria. “So, what President Tinubu is doing, I understand very well. Most people don’t understand. Most Nigerians don’t understand,” he said. He said the administration’s immediate objective was to stabilise the polity and create a conducive environment for economic activity. “First is to stabilise the polity, the entire polity, by bringing the price of foreign exchange to the playing table, and also bringing the price of fuel to the playing table, and bringing the environment to be conducive,” Kalu said. However, he acknowledged that while there had been progress at the macroeconomic level, Nigerians continued to face difficulties at the microeconomic level, particularly because of insecurity. He said insecurity had prevented some Nigerians from farming and working in parts of the North, South-East and other parts of the country. Subsidy return not an option, says Kalu Kalu also faulted calls by some political leaders for the restoration of petroleum subsidy, arguing that government should consider alternative measures to cushion the impact of economic hardship. He said his position was informed by his political experience and exposure to the petroleum business. “I was seeing some of our leaders saying they should bring back subsidy. I say it’s a laughing stock for anybody… I have two tank farms. I have tank farm in Akwa Ibom, Cross River, and I have palm farm in Lagos. “And I believe that bringing back subsidy is not best for Nigerians. It’s not an option to the economic development of Nigeria. Government can do other things, not fuel subsidy,” he said. Kalu also alleged that the former subsidy regime had been affected by fraudulent practices, claiming that some of the companies involved were not genuine. “We were about 143 companies that were doing subsidy, and I can tell you that half of the 143 were fake,” he alleged. He further said the removal of subsidy had reduced what he described as conspicuous spending associated with the former arrangement. “And while it was running… I can tell you that, you can see the level of private jets have reduced in Nigeria because there’s no more subsidy,” he said. Kalu praised Tinubu for taking what he described as a difficult but necessary decision. “So, President Tinubu took a major decision that most people cannot take, and this is what Nigeria requires,” he said. Kalu seeks security reforms While defending the administration’s economic reforms, Kalu said Tinubu still had significant work to do, particularly in restoring security and creating conditions for economic growth. “But President Tinubu have a lot of work to be done in the next couple of months and years, is to reform, to bring back the security dynamics back to normal,” he said. According to him, Nigeria had reached a stage where the focus should shift from stabilisation to economic growth, with improved security enabling farmers and businesses to return fully to productive activities. He identified insecurity, rural economic activity and local government autonomy as critical areas requiring attention. “What we need for the growth is to fight insecurity, farmers will go back to farm, people will go back to work in the rural areas, local government will have autonomy, local government councils will start disbursing money, and society will become normal,” Kalu said. The senator also appealed to Nigerians, particularly those from the South-East, to avoid dividing their political votes along ethnic lines. He urged his audience to support the APC and work towards political consolidation rather than division. “So, I will also appeal to you people to support our party. To support us,” he said. Kalu called for greater unity and cooperation among Nigerians, saying the country needed collaboration to overcome its challenges. “This is the time for consolidation for the government of Nigeria, for the people of Nigeria. There’s a lot of hatred among us as Igbos, as Nigerians, as people of faith. We must love ourselves, we need love more than quarreling. “We need assistance more than fighting. We need hands to help each other. We need to be the brother’s keeper that we need to keep,” he said. The post 2027: Kalu mobilises diaspora support for Tinubu, Hamzat appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: British actor Noel Clarke charged with sexual offences against five women
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye British actor Noel Clarke has been charged with sexual offences including sexual assault, voyeurism and exposure in connection with allegations involving five women. According to the BBC, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) authorised the Metropolitan Police to charge the 50-year-old Doctor Who and Kidulthood star on Wednesday following an investigation that began a year ago. Clarke, who is from Kensington, west London, faces two counts of sexual assault, three counts of voyeurism and one count of exposure. The alleged offences are said to have taken place between 2007 and 2016 and relate to five women. Clarke has not publicly responded to the charges. In a statement, the CPS said its prosecutors had established that there was sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that doing so was in the public interest. The investigation began after a man, then in his 40s, was arrested on 25 September 2025. A file of evidence was subsequently submitted to the CPS, which authorised the charges. Clarke is scheduled to appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on October 21 at 10:00 BST. Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney, who is leading the investigation, said the women connected to the charges were receiving support from specially trained officers. He also urged anyone who had been a victim of sexual assault to contact the police, assuring potential victims that information would be handled sensitively. Clarke rose to fame playing Mickey Smith in Doctor Who between 2005 and 2010. He later established himself as an actor, writer, producer and director. The post British actor Noel Clarke charged with sexual offences against five women appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Mines : la Guinée pose les bases d’un Fonds souverain doté de 4 milliards USD entre 2029 et 2035
items.description: La Guinée veut transformer une partie des revenus tirés de ses ressources minières en investissements durables et en épargne pour les générations futures. Le gouvernement a présenté, ce mercredi 9 septembre 2026, les grandes orientations du futur Fonds souverain de Guinée (FSG), appelé notamment à accompagner le Programme Simandou 2040. Réunis autour du Premier ministre Amadou Oury Bah et de la ministre de l’Économie, des Finances et du Budget, Mariama Ciré Sylla, des membres du gouvernement, cadres de l’administration, représentants du secteur privé, partenaires techniques et financiers et experts ont examiné l’architecture envisagée pour cette nouvelle institution. Selon les éléments présentés par le directeur du Bureau de stratégie et de développement (BSD), Mamadou Saliou Diallo, le Fonds devrait être constitué sous la forme d’une société anonyme à capitaux publics, détenue à 100 % par l’État. Les projections prévoient 4 milliards de dollars de dotations entre 2029 et 2035. L’objectif affiché est de rendre le Fonds opérationnel dès 2026, parallèlement à la montée en puissance des exportations de minerai de fer de Simandou. Trois missions : investir, stabiliser et épargner Le dispositif envisagé repose sur trois compartiments distincts. Le premier sera consacré à l’investissement et au développement, notamment dans la transformation minière, l’agro-industrie, les infrastructures productives et l'émergence de champions nationaux. Le deuxième aura une fonction de stabilisation. Il devra permettre d’amortir les conséquences de la volatilité des cours des matières premières sur les recettes publiques. Enfin, un compartiment d’épargne intergénérationnelle devra constituer progressivement un patrimoine diversifié, notamment à l’international, destiné à survivre à l’épuisement des ressources minières. Pour Mariama Ciré Sylla, l'enjeu consiste précisément à éviter que l'exploitation actuelle des ressources épuisables ne bénéficie qu'aux générations présentes. « Une partie des revenus de nos ressources naturelles sera préservée au bénéfice de ceux qui viendront après nous. C'est peut-être la dimension la plus exigeante de ce projet : accepter de mettre de côté aujourd'hui pour que demain soit plus solide », a-t-elle déclaré. La ministre a également insisté sur la vocation de développement du mécanisme. Les revenus miniers, a-t-elle soutenu, devront se traduire notamment par des infrastructures, des services de santé et d'éducation ainsi que des emplois. Raffineries, aciérie et agro-industrie parmi les investissements envisagés Les premières pistes présentées donnent une place importante à la transformation locale des matières premières. Figurent notamment parmi les projets envisagés des raffineries d'alumine, une aciérie d'une capacité de 500 000 tonnes par an et une raffinerie d'or d'une capacité annoncée de 250 000 à 500 000 kilogrammes par an. Le dispositif pourrait également soutenir des parcs agro-industriels utilisant les infrastructures du corridor de Simandou, une école de formation en alumine à Conakry, la modernisation de l'Institut supérieur des mines et de la géologie de Boké ainsi que le renforcement des capacités des PME guinéennes. Agriculture, élevage, pêche, santé, éducation et formation à travers la Simandou Academy, mais également tourisme, culture et artisanat apparaissent aussi dans les domaines susceptibles de bénéficier des investissements. Le Fonds est présenté comme l'un des instruments financiers devant accompagner Simandou 2040, programme comprenant, selon les données exposées, 122 mégaprojets, 36 réformes et plus de 200 milliards de dollars d'investissements projetés à l'horizon 2040, dont plus de 65 milliards durant la phase d'accélération 2025-2030. Le FSG n'a toutefois pas vocation à financer à lui seul ces 200 milliards de dollars. Il est plutôt présenté comme un outil destiné à mobiliser et attirer d'autres capitaux autour de projets jugés rentables sur les plans économique, social et financier. « Il investit, il ne dépense pas » Les concepteurs insistent également sur ce que le futur Fonds ne devra pas devenir. Il ne s'agira ni d'une caisse dans laquelle l'État pourra puiser librement en cas de difficulté budgétaire, ni d'un guichet de subventions. Le principe présenté est celui d'un investisseur de long terme : chaque franc engagé devra générer un retour sous forme de dividendes, de remboursement ou de création de valeur. Les financements pourront s'étendre sur 10, 15 ou 20 ans, contre des horizons généralement plus courts pour les banques commerciales. Le FSG pourrait investir aux côtés d'acteurs privés guinéens ou étrangers afin de partager les risques et de mobiliser des financements supplémentaires. Bah Oury met en garde contre les pressions du court terme Dans son intervention, le Premier ministre a surtout insisté sur la discipline qui devra entourer la gestion de cette institution. « Les ressources issues du Simandou ne devront jamais être absorbées par les seules urgences du présent », a averti Amadou Oury Bah. Elles devront, selon lui, soutenir la diversification économique, renforcer les capacités d'investissement du pays et préserver une partie de la richesse nationale au profit des générations futures. Le chef du gouvernement demande notamment des règles précises concernant les versements et les retraits, une gouvernance reposant sur la compétence et la responsabilité ainsi qu'une publication régulière des informations relatives à la gestion du Fonds. « Les ressources qui lui seront confiées appartiennent à la Nation. Leur gestion devra pouvoir être justifiée, documentée et évaluée », a-t-il insisté. Cette question de gouvernance constitue l'un des principaux enjeux du projet. Le gouvernement annonce vouloir aligner le FSG sur les principes de Santiago, référentiel international de bonnes pratiques applicable aux fonds souverains. Comment les projets seront-ils sélectionnés ? Le mécanisme présenté prévoit plusieurs étapes avant qu'un projet ne bénéficie d'un investissement : vérification de son éligibilité, analyse des risques opérationnels, financiers et juridiques, examen de sa rentabilité et de son impact, structuration du financement, approbation puis suivi. Les secteurs prioritaires cités comprennent notamment la transformation manufacturière et métallurgique, l'agriculture et l'agro-industrie, le BTP et le logement, la logistique et les transports, l'énergie et l'eau, le tourisme, le numérique et l'industrie financière. Pour les opérations les plus importantes, celles dépassant 5 % du bilan du Fonds, l'approbation relèverait du conseil d'administration. En dessous de ce seuil, la décision pourrait être déléguée à la direction exécutive. À l'issue de l'atelier, le gouvernement entend désormais consolider le cadre juridique et institutionnel, préciser la doctrine d'investissement et arrêter la feuille de route devant conduire à l'opérationnalisation du Fonds. Pour Bah Oury, la réussite du mécanisme se mesurera surtout sur le long terme : « Notre génération sera jugée sur l'usage qu'elle aura fait des ressources exceptionnelles confiées à la Guinée. »

items.title: Le Roi Mohammed VI condamne « l’agression criminelle iranienne » contre la Jordanie
items.description: Le Roi Mohammed VI a adressé, selon un communiqué du Cabinet royal, un message de solidarité et de condamnation au Roi Abdallah II Ibn Al Hussein, Souverain du Royaume hachémite de Jordanie, à la suite des attaques iraniennes répétées visant le pays frère. Dans son message, le Souverain affirme : « J’ai suivi avec une profonde préoccupation et indignation la nouvelle des attaques de missiles iraniennes, qui ont ciblé le territoire du Royaume hachémite de Jordanie frère, dans le prolongement de l’attitude hostile de l’Iran à l’égard de votre pays frère ainsi que des États arabes du Golfe. » « Face à cet événement grave, je tiens à exprimer à Votre Majesté ma ferme condamnation et mon profond rejet de cette agression criminelle et injustifiée, qui vise à porter atteinte à la stabilité de votre pays frère et à semer la terreur et l’inquiétude quant à la sécurité et à l’intégrité du peuple jordanien » , poursuit le Roi Mohammed VI. Le Souverain réaffirme également « la solidarité absolue du Royaume du Maroc avec le Royaume hachémite de Jordanie frère et son soutien constant et inconditionnel à toutes les mesures prises par les autorités jordaniennes, sous votre sage conduite, pour défendre la sécurité et la stabilité de la Jordanie ainsi que la sécurité de ses citoyens ». Le Roi Mohammed VI souligne à cet égard que « la sécurité de la Jordanie est partie intégrante de celle du Maroc ». En conclusion, le Souverain fait part de sa confiance dans le fait que « le peuple jordanien, sous votre conduite éclairée, saura surmonter les conséquences de ces attaques criminelles, grâce à la détermination, à la solidarité et au sang-froid qui le caractérisent ». The post Le Roi Mohammed VI condamne « l’agression criminelle iranienne » contre la Jordanie appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: More students benefited under Mahama gov’t than previous 20 years combined – SLTF CEO
items.description: The Chief Executive Officer of the Student Loan Trust Fund (SLTF), Dr Saajida Shiraz, says more students have benefited from government’s student support interventions under the Mahama administration than the total number supported during the previous 20 years of the Fund’s existence. Speaking on JoyNews’ The Pulse , she attributed the development to increased government prioritisation of tertiary education financing and the expansion of support programmes for students. “I would tell you that 20 years after the setup of the fund, it is changing lives, and exceptionally so in this last year, or under this government, because I can say that under this government, more students have benefited than the totality of the 20 years prior to this government’s coming into office. Altogether. I tell you that, “she stated on Wednesday, September 9. Dr Shiraz said the Student Loan Trust Fund has significantly expanded its reach, with thousands of students benefiting from enhanced loans and other interventions. According to her, the Fund has disbursed GH¢210 million in enhanced student loans to 59,300 students this year alone. “This year, because of government prioritisation, we have met all the demands for student loans,” she said. Dr Shiraz explained that the support goes beyond the traditional student loan scheme, with government also expanding assistance through the Student Loan Plus initiative. She said 1,997 students benefited from Student Loan Plus, including 626 students enrolled at the Ghana School of Law, whose fees were paid directly to the institution. The initiative, she noted, followed President John Mahama’s directive to extend student loan coverage to students pursuing professional legal education. About GH¢20 million was spent on the fees of the 626 Ghana School of Law students, she disclosed. Dr Shiraz further revealed that “the Fund has spent GH¢10 million to support tertiary students with disabilities, covering tuition and residential payments.” She said government is also working on policy modalities to provide additional support, including stipends and assistive learning devices for students with disabilities. The CEO identified the no-academic-fee policy as the largest area of expenditure, with approximately GH¢916 million spent across the 2024/2025 and 2025/2026 academic years. She said 152,000 students benefited during the first academic year, “while approximately 169,000 students have benefited during the current academic year.” Dr Shiraz noted that a small number of students are still undergoing data verification because of mismatches between their records and information held by the National Identification Authority. She explained that the additional checks are necessary to ensure that public funds are disbursed only to eligible beneficiaries.

items.title: Kafra : le Niger avance avec prudence vers un nouveau potentiel pétrolier…
items.description: Niamey, 9 septembre 2026 – Le Niger entend poursuivre l’évaluation du bloc pétrolier de Kafra avec « prudence, transparence et détermination », afin de transformer son potentiel en une source durable de souveraineté énergétique, de recettes et d’emplois au profit des Nigériens, a déclaré mercredi le ministre du Pétrole, Hamadou Tini. Lors d’un point de presse consacré à la campagne de forage lancée le 13 février 2026, le ministre a rappelé que le programme en cours prévoit le forage de quatre puits d’exploration sur une période de deux ans. Cette phase s’inscrit dans une autorisation d’exploration prorogée jusqu’au 3 juillet 2028. « Il serait prématuré de donner aujourd’hui une date certaine du premier baril », a prévenu M. Tini. Selon lui, une éventuelle mise en production dépendra notamment des résultats des forages, de la confirmation des volumes, de la productivité des réservoirs, de la faisabilité technique, des infrastructures à réaliser et des financements à mobiliser. Le gouvernement, a-t-il assuré, veut avancer rapidement, mais sans précipitation. « Dans le pétrole, une mauvaise décision prise très tôt peut coûter beaucoup plus cher qu’une bonne décision prise au bon moment », a souligné le ministre. Les travaux déjà réalisés sur le bloc de Kafra ont permis d’identifier plusieurs découvertes et un potentiel pétrolier jugé important. Les réserves 2P liées à une découverte effectuée sur le bloc avaient été estimées à environ 255 millions de barils en 2018. Une étude prospective conduite en 2023 dans la partie nord du bloc a, par ailleurs, évalué les ressources prospectives à environ 2,5 milliards de barils. Le ministre a toutefois insisté sur le caractère encore hypothétique de ce chiffre, soumis aux incertitudes géologiques et aux risques propres à l’exploration. « Kafra est encore dans une phase d’exploration et d’évaluation », a-t-il expliqué, précisant que les quatre puits programmés doivent fournir des données supplémentaires sur la qualité des réservoirs, leur étendue, leur productivité et la viabilité économique d’un futur développement. Le site recèle également un réservoir distinct d’huile lourde, dont les volumes sont estimés, sous réserve d’études complémentaires, à près de 168 millions de barils. Ce potentiel pourrait, à terme, contribuer à l’alimentation d’une unité de production de bitume destinée aux marchés nigérien et régional des matériaux routiers. Le bloc présente aussi un potentiel d’huile paraffinique susceptible d’intéresser les filières pharmaceutiques et pétrochimiques. Pour Hamadou Tini, l’enjeu de Kafra dépasse la seule perspective d’une production de pétrole. Le projet doit contribuer à la création de valeur nationale, à travers l’application de la loi sur le contenu local, le transfert de compétences, le renforcement des entreprises nigériennes et la maîtrise progressive des données et savoir-faire du secteur. « Avec Kafra, le Niger n’attend pas seulement un nombre de barils, nous attendons une création de valeur nationale », a affirmé le ministre. Les volumes officiels actualisés ne seront communiqués qu’après consolidation, certification et validation des résultats techniques et économiques, conformément aux normes reconnues dans l’industrie pétrolière. Le projet Kafra est localisé dans la zone désertique du nord du Niger, dans la région d’Agadez, entre les départements d’Iferouane et de Bilma, à environ 85 kilomètres de la frontière sud de l’Algérie. Le bloc, qui couvre 11 467 kilomètres carrés, abrite notamment le puits d’exploration Kafra Sud-Est 1. L’exploration pétrolière dans cette zone remonte aux années 1970, avec les forages historiques de Séguédine 1 en 1974 et de Tiffa 1 en 1975. Depuis 2005, Sipex, filiale du groupe algérien Sonatrach, participe aux activités sur le bloc. Les travaux ont permis l’acquisition, le traitement et l’interprétation d’environ 2 205 kilomètres de données sismiques 2D et de 760 kilomètres carrés de sismique 3D. Deux puits d’exploration ont ensuite été forés en 2018 et 2019, avant l’actualisation du cadre du projet en 2022. La prorogation de l’autorisation d’exploration et le lancement de la nouvelle campagne de quatre forages marquent ainsi une nouvelle étape dans l’évaluation du potentiel de Kafra. L’ambition affichée par les autorités est que ce projet génère des emplois, des recettes, des compétences et de nouvelles opportunités pour les Nigériens, dans le cadre d’une coopération renforcée avec l’Algérie. Source : Ministère du Pétrole et ANP L’article Kafra : le Niger avance avec prudence vers un nouveau potentiel pétrolier… est apparu en premier sur Tamtaminfo .

items.title: Droits des femmes : Le féminicide et l’avortement médicalisé au cœur des échanges avec le ministre de la Justice
items.description: Le ministre de la Justice, Garde des Sceaux, Me Moussa Sarr, a reçu, lundi 7 septembre 2026, une délégation d’organisations féminines et féministes. Les échanges ont porté sur plusieurs revendications relatives aux droits des femmes et des filles, notamment la reconnaissance du féminicide, la réforme du Code de la famille et l’avortement médicalisé en cas de viol et d’inceste. La question des droits des femmes s’est invitée, lundi, au ministère de la Justice. Me Moussa Sarr, Garde des Sceaux, a reçu une délégation composée de plusieurs organisations féminines et féministes engagées dans la défense et la promotion des droits des femmes et des filles. Parmi les participantes figuraient notamment Aminata Diallo, représentant Actrices Culturelles Ensemble (ACE), Maïmouna Yade et Oussama Sagna de J-Gen Sénégal, la sociologue Selly Ba, des représentantes du Réseau des Féministes du Sénégal et du Collectif des Féministes du Sénégal. Des organisations telles que l’Association des juristes sénégalaises (AJS), le Collectif Dafadoy, Roajelf, Pencum Ndakarou et Libéra étaient également représentées. La rencontre a permis aux organisations de présenter les travaux préparatoires aux assises nationales envisagées sur les droits des femmes et des filles. Elles ont également plaidé pour l’instauration d’un cadre permanent de dialogue et de concertation entre l’État et les organisations de la société civile. Le féminicide au cœur des revendications Plusieurs préoccupations ont été soulevées au cours des échanges. Les organisations ont notamment demandé la reconnaissance du féminicide comme une infraction autonome, au regard de la spécificité des violences meurtrières visant les femmes. La refonte du Code de la famille ainsi que l’accès à l’avortement médicalisé dans les cas de viol et d’inceste ont également figuré parmi les principaux sujets abordés. La situation des femmes détenues, les violences faites aux femmes et aux enfants et le harcèlement, notamment en ligne, ont aussi été évoqués. Les représentantes ont, par ailleurs, insisté sur la nécessité de renforcer la prise en charge des victimes et la formation des forces de sécurité. Elles ont salué l’action des Maisons de Justice, tout en appelant à leur affecter davantage de moyens. « Une attention particulière » aux préoccupations En réponse aux différentes préoccupations, Me Moussa Sarr a assuré qu’elles feraient l’objet d’une attention particulière. Il a notamment annoncé que la question des violences faites aux femmes et aux filles sera prise en compte dans le cadre de la circulaire de politique pénale générale. Sur la reconnaissance du féminicide, le ministre s’est déclaré, « a priori », favorable à une consécration spécifique de cette infraction. Les questions relatives à la réforme du Code de la famille et à l’avortement médicalisé en cas de viol et d’inceste appellent, selon le Garde des Sceaux, davantage de réflexion. Il a souligné le caractère sensible de ces sujets et appelé à poursuivre les échanges afin de parvenir à des « compromis dynamiques » prenant en compte les différentes opinions au sein de la société sénégalaise. Vers un cadre permanent de concertation Me Moussa Sarr a également réaffirmé la volonté de son département de considérer les organisations de défense des droits humains comme des « partenaires privilégiés de l’État ». Dans cette perspective, il a annoncé la mise en place prochaine d’un cadre de concertation et de dialogue réunissant les organisations de défense des droits humains au moins une fois par an. L’objectif sera notamment de faire le point sur la situation des droits humains au Sénégal. Le ministre a, en outre, évoqué l’étude d’un comité ad hoc chargé de préparer une stratégie nationale en matière de droits humains. La rencontre s’est achevée sur la volonté partagée de poursuivre le dialogue autour de la protection et de la promotion des droits des femmes et des filles. Arame NDIAYE

items.title: Govt hikes petrol price by Rs3.40, diesel by Rs6.72
items.description: Pakistan fuel prices, 2026 Official ex-depot prices (PKR/litre) — OGRA & Ministry of Energy notifications Petrol (MS-92) Diesel (HSD) Pre-crisis baseline Source: OGRA / Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division); Dawn.com · "> The government on Wednesday increased the price of petrol by Rs3.40 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs6.72 per litre. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs367.75 per litre while HSD will cost Rs392.67 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will be applicable on Sept 10 (Thursday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. On July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

items.title: Inside the White House on 9/11
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum is joined by John McConnell, the longtime senior speechwriter for President George W. Bush and Vice President Dick Cheney, to discuss their memories of September 11, 2001—25 years later. Then, David ends with a discussion of American Pastoral, a novel by Philip Roth, and what we can learn about domestic terrorism from the book. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Frum: Well, what I remember, that’s actually maybe one of my most vivid memories of the day, is stepping out of that building and Washington is deserted, and there’s yellow tape everywhere marking off the streets, and there’s the National Guard and armored personnel carriers everywhere. But the flags are still flying. They’ll be lowered the next—I remember thinking, They will be lowered tomorrow. But tonight they’re high. [ Music ] Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be John McConnell, a colleague of mine in the George W. Bush speechwriting department, and himself chief speechwriter to former Vice President Dick Cheney. We’ll be talking about 9/11 at the quarter-century anniversary. John and I spent much of the day together on 9/11, 2001—and we’ll be discussing what we saw, what we thought, what we felt, and what we did. The book discussion this week will also be terrorism-related: the novel American Pastoral by Philip Roth, his discussion of a homegrown terrorist in Roth’s own native state of New Jersey. Before either the dialogue or the book discussion, some home news. We’re going to be conducting an experiment here in The David Frum Show with a new tempo. Twice a week: releasing one show on Wednesday, the show you see, which will contain an interview and a book discussion, and a shorter show, which we’ll be releasing each Saturday on both YouTube and on whatever audio platform you use: Spotify, Apple, whatever it is. The second show, the Saturday show, will be much shorter—no interview, just some thoughts from me on the events of the week just passed. And the first of the shows, which we’ll release this coming Saturday, I will offer my own reflections on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. The United States has been almost unceasingly at war in the Middle East since 9/11, 2001. And I’ll be offering some of my thoughts about how I think about that experience, how others might want to think about it, whatever information I can offer. I played a small part in that history, and I think about it almost all the time, and I’ll be sharing those thoughts with you. And we’ll be continuing each Saturday after that. I do hope you’ll join and will bookmark us or subscribe to The Atlantic YouTube channel, or whatever audio channel you use, so you will not miss any of our Saturday shows. So that’s the news. I hope you will join me this coming Saturday and each successive Saturday for the second, shorter David Frum Show weekend episode. And now my dialogue with John McConnell. [ Music ] Frum: My guest today is John McConnell. John is one of the greatest speechwriters in American history, but that’s only incidentally why I’ve invited him today. John was a colleague in the George W. Bush administration, and I spent much of September 11th, 2001, in his company, sharing emotions of shock, dismay, and grief. As we mark the 25th anniversary of a tragic day, I wanted to be with him again. John wrote for Vice President Dan Quayle, then for the Bob Dole for President campaign in 1996. He joined the George W. Bush campaign in 2000 and then did remarkable service in the Bush White House, where he doubled as both a writer for the president and the sole speechwriter for Vice President Richard Cheney. John was a pallbearer at Vice President Cheney’s funeral. It was his frequent writing partner, Matt Scully, who delivered the finest verdict on John’s work: “As a general rule in Bush speeches, if the writing is graceful, judicious, and understated and makes you think about the subject at hand instead of anyone’s particular craftsmanship or religiosity, there’s a better-than-even chance it is by John McConnell.” It’s John’s lifelong reflex to deflect attention from himself, but today he must overcome that reflex and accept his place in American history. Thank you, John, for joining me today. John McConnell: Hello, David. Great to see you. Frum: So we spent the day together on 9/11. Let me start by asking you to summon your memories of what happened that day, where you were at, from the beginning to the end. McConnell: I was sitting outside Vice President Cheney’s inner office door in the West Wing. The night before, Matthew Scully and I had been working on a speech for the president for the end of that week. And at the end of Monday, I looked at my list of things to do, and I realized that Cheney had a speech on Friday too, and I thought, Well, I haven’t given this much thought. I should go talk to him. So I called his secretary. I said, Can I pop in on him tomorrow morning? And she said, How much time do you need? I said, Ten minutes, maybe five. I just wanted to ask him about his speech. And she said, Sure. Come at 8:30. And so the next morning—you remember how we’d get to the office, and the president’s and vice president’s schedules would be under our doors. And I looked at it; it said, “Meeting with John McConnell, 8:30,” and I thought, Oh, well, it’s an official meeting, so I really better be there at 8:30 sharp. So I went over, and the vice president was there. Sean O’Keefe, who was at the time the deputy director of the budget, former secretary of the Navy, friend of Cheney’s, had popped in on Cheney after the senior staff meeting. and so he was in there, and I waited outside the door. And I was just chatting with the vice president’s secretary’s personal aide and the Secret Service man standing post. And then about 8:46, I’m still waiting for the vice president. We’re seeing on television early reports that a plane has hit the World Trade Center, and so we’re just watching that and speculating what could possibly have gone wrong on this beautifully, perfectly clear late-summer day. Well, not long after we started seeing these pictures, that phone at the Secret Service command point outside the vice president’s office—the phone with no keys on it that just said Secret Service only —rang. And the agent standing post picked it up and listened for a few moments and said, Okay , and put it down. And he looked at me and told me that it was a passenger jet, a big commercial flight, that had hit the North Tower. And that was the first sense of real dread that this might be a coordinated event. And around that time the vice president’s visitor, Sean O’Keefe, walked out, and Cheney motioned me in. So it’s close to 9:00 at this point, and I go in and, and he says Good morning, John. I said, Sir, just need a couple minutes of your time to talk about this little thing we’ve got on Friday. He said, Sure; have a seat. But all we did was immediately turn to his television and just look at it. It was on, and so he was aware of what was happening in New York. And instead of talking about the matter I brought or hoped to raise with him, we just sat there looking at the TV, and it wasn’t very long until we saw the live image of the second plane coming in and slamming into the South Tower. And, of course, at that moment you realize that this is a terrorist attack. And he picked up the phone, and the president, as you recall, was out of town. He was in Florida. The vice president picked up the phone and asked to be connected to the president, as I recall. Then he got out of his chair and went out to see Andy Card’s assistant, the chief of staff’s assistant, to tell him to get in touch when he could. And then he came back in the office. And then I remember [Republican strategist] Mary Matalin came in, [the vice president’s chief of staff] Scooter Libby came in, [assistant to the president] Josh Bolten, [National Security Adviser] Condi Rice. And at a certain point, I realized there were going to be some big, big discussions. I remember also the president being on the phone with the vice president, and I had my hands on Cheney’s desk, and he was on the phone with the president, and I couldn’t make out what was being said even though I was right there. It was just a very low, a serious conversation between the president and vice president. But at a certain point, I left and I went to my office, and I went to the phone. Frum: Your office is in the Executive Office Building on the second floor? McConnell: That’s right, in the Eisenhower Building. And so it was just across that little West Executive Drive. And I picked up the phone, and I called my mom, who was here where I am today in northernmost Wisconsin, a place called Bayfield County. And I called her, and she said, Where are you? And I said, I’m in my office, and everything’s fine. And she says, Well, on television it says the White House is being evacuated. And I remember I kind of chuckled. I said, Well, I’m here. And nobody knows you better than your mother, and she knows my passive personality. She said, John, go out in the hallway and see if anyone else is there. Frum: ( Laughs .) McConnell: And I said, Okay, okay. I will, I will, and I’ll call you. And I put the phone down, and I went out into the hallway. And sure enough, people were being told, Get out, get out. And so I went down the stairs and then down outside, they call them the Navy Steps, which you know well, the steps from the Eisenhower Building going down. Basically directing you right into the West Wing there, across that little West Executive Drive. And I saw one of the vice president’s Secret Service men who I’d known for a long time, and he said, John, everybody’s got to get out of here. And I said, I’m going. And then just a second or two later, one of the uniformed Secret Service guys comes running from the direction of the White House, down that little set of steps near the West Wing entrance, and said, Everybody run! There’s a plane coming at us! And I don’t remember running, but I remember just pointing north and going up West Executive Drive, and it was then that I saw a big plane over 16th Street. And I remember thinking in that moment, I swear to God, I thought, That plane is filled with people. It’s about to slam into the White House, kill them all, and destroy the White House. I cannot believe this is the year 2001. And that was the instant thought that came to my mind. I just can’t believe this is happening. And we later found out that it was thought for a while that that was the plane that ended up hitting the Pentagon, but the Pentagon had already been hit at that point. So that plane I saw over 16th had to be a diverted commercial aircraft. I just assume that’s what it was. And so we’re out there. Nobody knows where to go. There’s no evacuation plan. The White House has never been evacuated. And so, I ended up just out—you know, you leave the White House complex, you’re on West Executive Drive, and then boom, there’s Lafayette Park. And if you walk for one minute, you’re on Connecticut Avenue. And that’s about where I met up with you, isn’t it, David? Frum: That’s exactly right. So let me tell you my memory up to that point. So as you say, the president was in Florida that day. So I was a little bit off duty, and so I played a little bit of hooky. Our older kids then went to a Jewish day school in Rockville, which is quite a distance from downtown D.C. And we shared often driving duties with a friend who had children in the same school. So that morning, I volunteered to take my children, Danielle’s and my children, and this friend’s children, to drive them up to Rockville, which is a long drive. And then you’re coming back with the rush-hour traffic. So I got to the White House quite late by White House standards. I would’ve got there about quarter to nine, and parked the car. I was walking toward the Executive Office Building, and my clunky mobile phone of those days rang, and it was my wife who said, There’s something—something terrible is happening. You should get to a television screen as close as you can. So I remember entering the Executive Building, going up the stairs that you just described going down, walking along—my office that I shared with Matt Scully was on a much busier corridor than yours. The plan of the Executive Office Building is like a big squared-off number eight. And Scully and I were on the short arm of the number eight, away from the White House on the 17th Street side. We had a huge office with a partition in between, part for him, part for me. I went to my office, and I remember walking along that corridor and hearing the sounds of every television set along the wall of increasingly agitated voices. I got to my office and turned on my television and sat down, and just as I sat down, it was your mother who called. Danielle called me a second time, my wife, Danielle—and this would’ve been about 10 past nine—and said, A second plane has hit the World Trade Center. They’re going to attack the White House. You need to get out of there. And my personality’s a little balkier than yours, and I remember saying to her, I am not leaving. I am not leaving. And I don’t know what I thought I was going to achieve by staying there. ( Laughs .) I was going to type with renewed fervor and patriotism. But what am I going to do? What am I doing? But sorry, No, I’m staying. And I said goodbye, and I sat down at my desk to do whatever the hell it was I thought I was going to do. And just at that moment, one of the uniformed Secret Service officers pounded on the door, because we were on a busy traffic corridor, so we were right at the center of all of the traffic toward the Navy Steps was going to flow by, or almost all of it was going to flow by the front door of the Scully and Frum suite. So they pound and say, Get out of here. And I stepped out of the office, and I remember the Secret Service officers in uniform saying, Don’t run. And so we began to walk briskly, and then two beats later they changed their tune. They said, Run! And they shouted, Ladies, if you can’t run in heels, kick off your heels! And we ran out across the crossbar to the Navy Steps, down the Navy Steps, as you say, up through Lafayette Square, and that’s where I met you. And we all realized at the same time that we had no way of communicating with the world. All the mobile phones were dead. The only thing that still worked were pagers, and I didn’t have one. One of the things that people may not recall today is in 2001, a phone was not part of your body the way it is today, that it was a much cludgier—all you could do with it was make phone calls, basically. And so you didn’t carry it around all the time the way people do today. So people were separated from their phones. But anyway, they didn’t work. Because everyone in the world, or everyone in Washington, D.C., anyway, was trying to get onto the same number of very finite circuits that existed in 2001 at the same time, and all the lines went dead. McConnell: Yeah, and that’s a very good point you make, David. If you weren’t around then, you know, if you’re 30 or less, you don’t know. I mean, we got BlackBerrys in 2004 when you could look at your email for the first time without being at your desk. But text messages, all that stuff, came much later in terms of just ordinary usage in everyone’s hand. Frum: I think there’s no social media of any kind. There’s no YouTube, there’s no Facebook, there’s no Twitter, nothing. And mobile computers do exist, but they’re pretty kludgy. So it’s still very much a deskbound world of communication. McConnell: Well, I remember when I was a kid reading about the day that President Kennedy was assassinated, and there was some vignettes of that day. And one of them was a blind beggar in New York City had a little pocket radio, and people were gathered around this man listening to that radio. And 9/11, it was still kind of that world. Because you had—I mean, you had 24-hour news on TV and stuff. But out on the street, I remember at one point during that day hearing a very loud car radio somewhere, maybe on our walk, David, and stopping momentarily to see if there was anything coming through that radio that we could learn. Frum: Yeah. Well, one of the reasons we’re all milling around, this is something I learned later. So 9/11, 2001—it’s only a dozen years after the end of the Cold War. And it’s at the end of a long period of security and peace. So the evacuation plans for the White House are still the Cold War plans, and the contingency that they planned for was a Soviet decapitation strike on the centers of government of the United States. And so the plan was: Get the president up in the air on Air Force One as fast as you can, so he can command whatever response is required to this Soviet decapitation strike. Get other key White House personnel into the tiny little bomb shelter underneath the West Wing that’s, I think, basically left over from the 1950s. So it has room for what? A dozen, 15 people. Get them down there, and then everybody else is going to be vaporized in the strike. Which is very sad for them, but it means you don’t need a plan as to where you’re going to put these people. ( Laughs. ) Because you assume not only are they all dead, but their bodies don’t exist anymore. McConnell: Right. ( Laughs. ) And you know, I never saw the bunker, obviously. I left the vice president’s office just before they realized that there was a plane coming directly at the White House at 500 miles an hour. And that’s when Jimmy Scott, the head of the vice president shift, ran into him and said, Sir, we have to leave. Frum: Yeah. McConnell: And Cheney said, All right. And he said, Now. Frum: So they’re taking him to the bunker, and that’s where Condoleezza Rice will go, and then the presidential entourage is on its way to Air Force One. In my opinion, probably his greatest novel. American Pastoral tells a story of an American Jew whose daughter gets mixed up in extremist activity. The novel is narrated by a man named Nathan Zuckerman, who’s Roth’s recurring literary alter ego. And Nathan Zuckerman tells a story of his childhood friend, Seymour “The Swede” Levov, a golden-boy athlete from Zuckerman and Roth’s hometown of Newark, New Jersey. The Swede seems to have it all. He’s a former high-school sports star. He marries a Miss New Jersey. He takes over his father’s successful glove-manufacturing business, and he settles into an idyllic life in rural Old Rimrock, New Jersey. He has one child, an adored daughter named Merry, M-E-R-R-Y. Merry becomes increasingly politically outspoken in the course of the 1960s, when the novel is set. She gets involved in radical causes. She becomes increasingly dogmatic. Merry has a speech impediment, and somehow that concentrates her rage into forms of action that are beyond speech. And ultimately, that expressed itself when, in order to oppose the Vietnam War, Merry plants a bomb in the local post office that kills a local doctor. Merry then disappears, goes underground, and The Swede spends years looking for her. When he finally tracks her down, she’s back in Newark, New Jersey, living in terrible filth and squalor, and she has converted to a form of ultra-pacifism. She becomes a Jain, J-A-I-N, a religion from India that is so opposed to violence that it refuses to kill even an insect. And The Swede has to contemplate how his beloved daughter could swing from one extreme of murder to this other extreme of pacifism almost beyond reason. The Swede, who’s had this perfect life—sheltered from everything, coasting on inherited prosperity and success on an American dream in a country that has been a golden land for Jews like himself—he has to confront this eruption of what Roth calls “the American berserk,” the country’s capacity to burst out from anybody’s planned order into these forms of strange, bizarre personal violence. Roth is here describing something very real. I mean, I went through, did a quick scroll through incidents that reminded me of the story of Merry Levov—of privileged people, people at every American advantage who lash out, who would adopt some scheme of or some personal ideology of extremist hate, and then lash out in violence against others. There’s so many examples of this. Let me just mention a few that just come to mind in the course of an ordinary search. Remember Elliot Rodger? Elliot Rodger was the son of a Hollywood director. He grew up in very comfortable circumstances. He developed this ideology of misogyny; incel , I think, is the term. Misogyny, violent hatred to women. He killed six people and wounded 14 in a rampage, leaving behind a manifesto justifying what he did. Or Patrick Crusius. He was the man who turned a weapon on a parking lot in El Paso to kill 23 people, motivated by his “Great Replacement,” anti-immigrant ideology. He also acted alone, and he also had a comfortable middle-class upbringing in Dallas, Texas. Or Luigi Mangione—this is a perfect example of this—who comes from a prominent family in Maryland, and he gunned down an insurance executive in New York City. Again, for some crazy, bizarre ideological reason all his own, that unfortunately has found resonance in some of the more malicious corners of online life. Or Ayman Mohamed Ghazali; I’ve talked about him before. He’s the Lebanese immigrant who settled in Michigan, was given the opportunity to make a life for himself in America, given the amazing gift of American citizenship, and instead took guns to Temple Israel in West Bloomfield. You know, these people all have motives. They may be diagnosable as having some kind of mental illness, but they’re not so delusional as not to understand what they’re doing. But they’re acting on some script, some sense of grievance—the American berserk that Roth talks about—that pushes them in these directions. And notice something else. They all have these remarkable resources and freedom. They have the resources to acquire weapons, and they have the freedom to conduct their work without surveillance. There are many societies in which people like this would be caught early because they lived in more of a surveillance state. Americans have freedom, resources. They have the ability to become whoever they are. And for most of us, the ability to become whoever we are is a great gift. It allows us to realize ourselves in all kinds of ways, in ways that people could not realize themselves even in countries that are comparably free but are not as supremely abundant and affluent as the United States. But when you’re given the right to be who you are, that reveals something in some people that is berserk, that is bad. It allows, it gives you more scope to be indulged in wickedness and cruelty and hatefulness, to come up with some crazy set of ideas all your own, or that link in some other way. And to act out against your fellows in ways that bring hurt and harm and sorrow and suffering to the human species. America gives all of us the means to be ourselves, and the question we all face is: Who will we be? That’s it for this week’s episode of The David Frum Show. Thanks so much for watching. As ever, please, the best way to support the work of the show, if you can, is by subscribing to The Atlantic. That helps me and all of my colleagues. Please also consider subscribing to our YouTube channel, or whatever social-media channel you enjoy the program on. Share it with others, and spread the word. See you next week on The David Frum Show. Bye-bye.

items.title: Gov’t reviewing policy for stipends, assistive devices for disabled students – SLTF CEO
items.description: The Chief Executive Officer of the Students Loan Trust Fund (SLTF), Dr Saajida Shiraz, has revealed that government is considering additional support measures, including the payment of stipends and the provision of assistive learning devices for tertiary students with disabilities. Dr Shiraz said the move forms part of ongoing efforts to improve support for students with disabilities pursuing tertiary education. Speaking on JoyNews’ The Pulse , Dr Shiraz said: “For the fee tertiary for persons with disabilities, we expended GH¢10 million so far to support the tuition and residential payment for these students.” According to her, the government is currently working through the necessary policy modalities to determine how additional support can be provided to beneficiaries. She said the proposed measures could include stipends to help students meet their day-to-day needs, as well as assistive learning devices to support their academic work. “Government also is going through the policy modalities for the payment of stipends and perhaps the provision of assistive learning devices,” Dr Shiraz added. The initiative, she noted, is aimed at complementing existing government support for students with disabilities and addressing some of the additional challenges they face in accessing tertiary education.

items.title: Israel sets deadline for Britain to close consulate as settlers warn of sanctions hit
items.description: Israel has given Britain 30 days to close its East Jerusalem consulate in response to sanctions on goods from settlements, a measure Britain’s leader said ‌on Wednesday was needed to “stand against injustice” in the occupied West Bank. In the West Bank, where Israeli settlements have eaten into territory Palestinians seek for a state, settler business owners said the sanctions — announced on Tuesday by Britain, France and Canada — would dent their revenues and at least one said they could force him to close his date farm. The sanctions are among the strongest collective actions taken by Western countries that Israel once counted ​as close allies, highlighting its growing isolation over the war in Gaza and expansion of settlements in occupied territory. ISRAEL SETS DEADLINE FOR BRITAIN TO CLOSE CONSULATE Two Israeli officials and two ​other sources familiar with the matter said London had been given 30 days to close its East Jerusalem consulate, which represents Britain in Jerusalem, ⁠the West Bank and Gaza on Palestinian issues. Israel has also barred 12 British politicians from visiting the country, told British officials and diplomats in the West Bank and a Gaza coordination ​centre in Israel to leave, and said Britain can no longer train Palestinian security forces in the West Bank. It has not yet announced actions against France or Canada, which joined Britain in ​saying they would halt trade with settlements, or against nine other countries that endorsed the UK sanctions. Although the UK sanctions were widely anticipated, Israeli parliamentary opposition leader Yair Lapid said on Tuesday that “no one knew” the other countries were going to endorse the move. Speaking before Britain’s parliament, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain had long endorsed the two-state solution for the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, but that words needed to be backed by action. “We will always ​stand with the underdog and take what action we can to support them,” he said. There has so far been a muted response from the United States, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio ​saying Washington did not want to see “anything destabilising” in the West Bank while declining to specifically comment on the UK sanctions. The U.S. ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, a staunch supporter of Israel, has condemned the ‌sanctions and ⁠accused the British government of “Jew hate”. U.S. President Donald Trump has not commented on the move. Israeli leaders have described the sanctions as “morally distorted”. Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, accused the UK of “blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and its electoral process”. Israel is due to hold a general election on October 27. ‘IF I CAN’T SELL TO EUROPE, I NEED TO CLOSE THE BUSINESS’ Much of the world views Israel’s settlements as illegal under international law. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has overseen a rapid expansion of small settler outposts, some of which have perpetrated violence against Palestinians. Israel rejects ​the assertion that the settlements are illegal, ​viewing the West Bank as disputed territory ⁠to which it holds biblical ties. Diplomats widely regard the sanctions as an important but symbolic step, with goods from Israeli settlements making up only a fraction of Israel’s exports. Still, Israelis working in West Bank settler agriculture businesses told Reuters the sanctions would bar their products from important markets ​in Europe. Yaakov Berg, head of the Psagot Winery near the Palestinian city of Ramallah, said Britain made up a big market for the ​winery, which exports around 60% ⁠of its wine. Israeli and Palestinian rights groups say the winery was established on privately owned Palestinian land. Berg said the sanctions were a reflection of antisemitic hate, something Britain and others reject. “Sometimes you suffer. Sometimes you lose some money. That’s okay with us. We are not going to change the truth and who we are because of a few dollars,” Berg said. In Kibbutz Almog, a Jordan Valley settlement ⁠south of ​the Palestinian town of Jericho, one of the area’s many settler date farmers, 59-year-old Moses Gazi, said the sanctions ​could end up hurting the many Palestinians he employs on his farm. “If I can’t sell my dates to Europe, I need to close the business. I close the business, each of (the Palestinian workers) has something like three, four, five ​kids. What are they going to do?” he said.
